claims.text: The initial phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy tends to crystallize under standard cooling conditions or has a thermally unstable amorphous phase.
Adding 1–3 at% of a secondary element can increase mixing entropy without drastically changing the overall composition.
Minimal high-entropy micro-alloying will improve glass-forming ability in a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy.
Minimal high-entropy micro-alloying will extend the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
The intervention should work when processing permits an entropy-dominated regime during the liquid-to-glass transition.
Excessive additive concentration may cause phase separation.
Extremely rapid quenching may eliminate the benefit because kinetics override thermodynamic stabilization.
Minimal alloying or increased alloying-element diversity reduces liquid fragility.
The structural changes lower resistance to crystallization.
Enhanced liquid mixing entropy reduces liquid fragility.
Reduced liquid fragility suppresses nucleation of crystalline phases during cooling.
Suppression of crystalline nucleation stabilizes the amorphous structure at elevated temperatures.
The modified alloy should have a higher glass-transition temperature than the additive-free control.
The modified alloy should exhibit a delayed crystallization onset during heating.
The modified alloy should exhibit reduced liquid fragility relative to the additive-free control.
Additive concentrations above the optimum may produce phase inhomogeneity or unintended crystalline compounds.

contradictions.description: The structural-mediator field says the intervention lowers resistance to crystallization, which implies easier crystallization, whereas the mechanism and predicted outcome assert suppressed crystallization and delayed crystallization onset.
